# Using Google Trends for SEO and content

Google presented three uses of Google Trends for content, marketing and SEO: keyword selection, scheduling and ideation. For keyword selection, compare candidate terms on the Explore page for the right country, region and time frame, use the higher-interest wording in titles and campaigns, and check both top and rising commonly searched queries. For scheduling, check whether your topics are seasonal in your own market rather than assuming (a five-year US chart showed umbrella interest peaking in June with sunscreen, not in winter), because a seasonal pattern predicts the next wave of interest and the time to have content ready. For ideation, Trending now surfaces events within about ten minutes, and Google said journalists use it every morning to find content gaps (not in Google's docs); Google's own Trends guide adds to follow trends only where the topic fits the business and its expertise. A Day 2 community talk made the same point for international sites: regional demand changes over time, as a chart of northern versus southern European interest in ceiling fans showed. On Day 3 a community speaker described using Trends to choose what to cover in depth when entering a new market, and Google's marketing research showed Trends charts of trust-checking searches such as 'is [brand] legit' rising since about 2020 in many markets and languages (said at the event).

Based on: `D2-C789`, `D2-C790`, `D2-C791`, `D2-C796`, `D2-C794`, `D2-C798`, `D2-C799`, `D2-C800`, `D2-C802`, `D2-C804`, `D2-C805`, `D2-C792`, `D2-C635`, `D2-C636`, `D3-C104`, `D3-C581`, `D3-C582`.

## What to do

- Compare candidate keywords in Trends for the exact country or region where the page should rank, and reuse the higher-interest wording in titles and headings.
- Map seasonality per target market and publish or refresh seasonal content a few weeks before the rise.
- Use rising queries to find emerging sub-topics worth a new page or section.
- Check Trending now for content gaps, but cover only trends that fit your business and expertise.
- Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year.
- After a launch or campaign, compare baseline interest before and after the spike.
- Track trust queries such as '[brand] legit' or '[brand] seriös' per market in Trends and Search Console, and answer them on the site.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Central guide to Google Trends says to use Trends to inform a content strategy only where a topic fits the business and its users, and to focus on terms where the site has expertise and experience.
  > "you shouldn't write about something just because it's trending"
  <br><sub>`D2-C792` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Google Trends · is the documentation · [Get started with Google Trends](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/trends-start)</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year, for example by comparing regions and seasons in Google Trends, because climate, housing or habits can shift what a market wants.
  <br><sub>`D2-C637` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** To judge a launch or campaign in Google Trends, compare the brand's baseline search interest before and after the spike, not only the height of the spike, because a lasting baseline lift is the durable gain.
  <br><sub>`D2-C775` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Before treating a spike in an ambiguous keyword as demand for your topic, zoom in on the period in Google Trends and check the commonly searched queries, since another meaning of the word (as with 'ai' in 2012) may be driving it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C781` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A Google Trends line that falls over many years is not proof that a market is shrinking; compare terms against each other in the same chart, and take absolute numbers from keyword tools or Search Console impressions.
  <br><sub>`D2-C788` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Compare candidate keywords in Google Trends for the exact country or region where the page should rank, because the higher-interest wording can differ between markets that share a language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C793` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** In Google Trends' commonly searched queries, rising queries point to emerging sub-topics worth a new page or section, while top queries show the established wording to reuse in titles and headings.
  <br><sub>`D2-C797` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Publish or refresh seasonal content a few weeks before the seasonal rise that Google Trends shows for each target country, so the pages are crawled and indexed before demand peaks.
  <br><sub>`D2-C803` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The regional search interest maps in Google Trends give a quick first check of demand by country or region before localising content for a new market.
  <br><sub>`D2-C817` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Google Trends</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Track trust queries about your brand, such as '[brand] legit', '[brand] reviews' or '[brand] seriös', in Search Console and Google Trends for each market, and answer them on the site, for example with a trust or about page, instead of leaving the answer to third-party review sites.
  <br><sub>`D3-C594` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Mastering the messy middle</sub>
